KP23 Decision Trees: OBCT, Splitting Criteria and Pruning

Level: undergraduate, year 3

Pattern Recognition | Chapter 4, §4.20

Slides: read and download

Learning objectives

  • Explain the structure of an OBCT and the four things fixed in training, and compute the impurity and the impurity decrease.
  • Explain why the children are weighted, what happens when a tree is too large and how pruning works.
  • Explain the high variance of decision trees and how bagging and random forests lower it.

KP23 Decision Trees: OBCT, Splitting Criteria and Pruning

One-sentence summary: Instead of drawing a complex boundary, ask a series of simple yes/no questions, each cutting the feature space once. The size of the tree is the key, a single tree has a high variance and bagging averages it out.

1. A series of yes/no questions

Plain explanation: Can classification skip the boundary and ask a series of simple yes/no questions?

  • Decision tree: a series of yes/no decisions along a path of nodes, ruling out classes step by step until a leaf is reached.

The most popular is the OBCT (ordinary binary classification tree): every node asks one feature, "xi≤αx_i\le\alphaxi​≤α?", cutting the space into hyper-rectangles parallel to the axes. Strengths: especially good with many classes; often not every feature has to be tested; simple and easy to interpret; numeric and categorical features both work.

Figure lec05-kp23-partition: three regions on the left and the matching tree on the right.

2. Four ingredients and the candidates

Training fixes four things: the set of candidate questions; the splitting criterion; the stop-splitting rule; the class-assignment rule for leaves. Candidates: if feature xkx_kxk​ has NtkN_{tk}Ntk​ distinct values in the node, take midpoints of neighbouring values as thresholds, at most Ntk−1N_{tk}-1Ntk​−1 (the book writes NtkN_{tk}Ntk​); over all features the list is finite. Example (designed here): 10 distinct values 1.0, 1.4, 2.2, …, 7.0 give 9 midpoints.

Figure lec05-kp23-cands: 10 values and 9 midpoints.

3. Impurity

Impurity (formal definition):

I(t)=−∑i=1MP(ωi∣t)log⁡2P(ωi∣t), I(t)=-\sum_{i=1}^{M}P(\omega_i|t)\log_2P(\omega_i|t), I(t)=−i=1∑M​P(ωi​∣t)log2​P(ωi​∣t),

larger the more mixed the classes in the node. It is maximal when all classes are equal (log⁡2M\log_2Mlog2​M for MMM classes) and 0 when all are of one class (with 0log⁡0=00\log0=00log0=0); probabilities are estimated by Nti/NtN_t^i/N_tNti​/Nt​. Examples: (4,4,2)(4,4,2)(4,4,2): 1.522 (the book writes 1.521); (1,1,1)(1,1,1)(1,1,1): log⁡23=1.585\log_23=1.585log2​3=1.585; (5,0,0)(5,0,0)(5,0,0): 0.

5. Why weighting

Example (designed here): a parent of 5 against 5 (I=1I=1I=1). Split A: Yes (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), No (4,5)(4,5)(4,5); split B: Yes (4,1)(4,1)(4,1), No (1,4)(1,4)(1,4). Weighted: A =0.108=0.108=0.108, B =0.278=0.278=0.278, so B is chosen. Unweighted (children simply averaged): A =0.504=0.504=0.504, B =0.278=0.278=0.278, so A is chosen; one pure point is mistaken for a big gain. Common misconception: a split is good whenever a child becomes pure; making only a tiny subset pure is worth little.

Figure lec05-kp23-weight: the scores of two splits with and without weighting.

6. How large a tree

Example (designed here): two noisy half-moons (sd 0.35), 100 training and 1000 new points per class, entropy criterion. Depth 1 (2 leaves): 76.5% training, 73.3% on new points; 2 (4): 89.0% / 83.7%; 4 (11): 90.0% / 82.2%; 8 (20): 99.0% / 85.2%; 12 (24): 100% / 85.1%. With more leaves training climbs to 100% while new points stay near 85%; a too-large tree learns the details of the training set.

Figure lec05-kp23-depth: tree depth and accuracy.

7. Pruning

Pruning: grow a large tree first, then cut branches that are not worth their cost, judged by an error estimate plus complexity such as the leaf count (the source says stopping on an impurity-decrease threshold often stops too early or too late). On the same data, with pruning strength α\alphaα: 0 gives 24 leaves, 100% training and 85.1% on new points; 0.01: 22 leaves, 85.1%; 0.02: 10 leaves, 96.5% / 87.3%; 0.05: 7 leaves, 94.0% / 86.3%. One dataset and one run, a gain of about 2 points. Entropy and Gini over 20 draws (depth 4) give 86.1±2.3% and 86.1±3.1% on new points: the criterion hardly matters (as the source says).

Figure lec05-kp23-prune: pruning strength and accuracy.

8. Variance and bagging

Bagging: draw BBB samples with replacement from the training set, grow a tree on each and take a majority vote. Variance (designed here): on 8 training sets of the same size every first cut is on the second feature, with thresholds 0.42, 0.11, 0.12, 0.09, 0.22, 0.26, 0.22, 0.29 and 22 to 33 leaves. Averages (20 training sets, new points): a single tree 84.4±1.4%; bagging with 25 trees 87.7±1.1%; a random forest (bagging plus random features per node) of 25 trees 87.8±1.1%. A tree is hierarchical, so an error high up reaches every leaf below; averaging lowers the variance. To remember: a decision tree makes hierarchical, sequential hard decisions while a neural network makes parallel soft ones; the MLP wins on error rate and the tree on training time (source).

Figure lec05-kp23-bag: the mean accuracy of three methods and 8 root thresholds.

Extension: oblique questions, practice and worked solution

Oblique questions (designed here): 300 points uniform on [−1,1]2[-1,1]^2[−1,1]2 with the class given by x1+x2>0x_1+x_2>0x1​+x2​>0; one oblique question x1+x2≤0x_1+x_2\le0x1​+x2​≤0 separates them exactly. Axis-parallel trees (3000 new points; 13 to 14 leaves are needed for about 95%): depth 1: 2 leaves, 75.0%; depth 3: 7, 89.6%; depth 6: 13, 95.4%; the full tree has 14 leaves, 100% training and 95.1% on new points. An oblique question ∑ckxk≤α\sum c_kx_k\le\alpha∑ck​xk​≤α cuts well but trains harder (source).

Figure lec05-kp23-oblique: the diagonal class boundary and the leaves of axis-parallel trees.
